title: ship vs sheep
tip: /ɪ/ is short and relaxed, lips loose. /iː/ is long and tight, lips spread like a smile. Hold the long one a little longer.
phrases: The ship carried a thousand sheep.
Please leave a little bit of cheese.
He felt a chill in his feet.

title: bad vs bed
tip: For /æ/ open your mouth wide and drop your jaw, as if saying 'a' in 'cat'. For /ɛ/ the mouth is more closed and the tongue higher.
phrases: The man sent ten pens.
My bad pen is on the bed.
Ann met a lad at the land office.

title: cut vs cot
tip: /ʌ/ is short, from the middle of the mouth, like a quick 'uh'. /ɑː/ (or /ɒ/) is open and rounder at the back: 'ah'.
phrases: The duck stuck in the dock.
A cup of luck for the cop.
Shut the lock before the bus leaves.

title: full vs fool
tip: /ʊ/ is short with relaxed lips. /uː/ is long with lips pushed forward into a small circle.
phrases: Pull the full pool cover.
He could not look at the new suit.
The cook took a good look at the food.

title: think vs sink
tip: For /θ/ put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and blow air. For /s/ keep the tongue behind the teeth.
phrases: I think the thick sink is sick.
Thank you for the math path.
Three thin things sank.

title: three vs tree
tip: /t/ is a quick tap of the tongue on the ridge behind the teeth. /θ/ is a soft stream of air with the tongue between the teeth.
phrases: Three thin trees stand there.
I thought the team taught the theme.
Thank the tenth team.

title: they vs day
tip: /ð/ is the voiced 'th': tongue between the teeth and your voice on. /d/ taps the ridge behind the teeth.
phrases: They went there then.
Though the dough is thick, breathe slowly.
That brother does this every day.

title: vest vs west
tip: For /v/ touch your top teeth to your bottom lip and buzz. For /w/ round your lips and do not touch the teeth.
phrases: The vet wore a wet vest.
We view the wine vine in the west.
Very well, we will visit Venice.

title: right vs light
tip: For /l/ press the tongue tip on the ridge behind the teeth. For /r/ curl the tongue back without touching anything and round your lips a little.
phrases: The red light led the right road.
A clown wore the crown on the grass.
Please collect the correct glass.

title: ship vs chip
tip: /ʃ/ is a smooth, long 'sh'. /tʃ/ starts with a stop (tongue on the ridge) and then releases into 'sh': 'ch'.
phrases: Share the cheap chips.
Watch the ship wash the shoes.
Catch the cash in the chair.

title: sea vs she
tip: /s/ is a thin hiss with the lips spread. /ʃ/ pulls the tongue back and rounds the lips a little for a wider, softer sound.
phrases: She sells sea shells.
Sort the short socks.
Save the sheet from the shock.

title: jet vs yet
tip: /dʒ/ starts with a stop and releases into 'zh': 'j'. /j/ is a gentle glide, like the start of 'yes'.
phrases: The jet is not here yet.
Yell the joke this year.
Jam and yam in January.

title: pan vs fan
tip: /p/ is a burst of air from closed lips. /f/ is a steady stream of air between the top teeth and bottom lip.
phrases: The fast fan fills the pan.
A fair pair of pine pins.
Past the pool is the fine pit.

title: bill vs pill
tip: Both close the lips. /b/ is voiced: feel your throat buzz. /p/ is voiceless and puffs air. Hold your hand in front of your mouth to feel it.
phrases: A big bear ate the pear.
Pack the bill in the back.
The pig put on the big cap.

title: ten vs den
tip: /t/ is voiceless with a small puff of air; /d/ is voiced. At the end of a word, a vowel before /d/ is held longer than before /t/.
phrases: Ten dogs ran down town.
Write about the bad bat.
The dame tied the tame deer.

title: cap vs gap
tip: Both are made at the back of the tongue. /k/ is voiceless with a puff of air; /g/ is voiced with your throat buzzing.
phrases: The goat wore a cold coat.
A girl keeps gold in a bag.
Come back to class with the glass.

title: hair vs air
tip: /h/ is a light breath before the vowel; do not drop it. Without it the word changes: 'hair' becomes 'air'.
phrases: Hold the old hat.
He can hear his ear ring.
The hill air is high and hot.

title: sing vs sin
tip: For /ŋ/ the back of the tongue touches the soft palate and the sound goes through the nose; do not add a 'g' sound or touch the front of the mouth.
phrases: The king sang a song.
A thing rang in the morning.
Singing brings many things.
